```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
has_mvt <- requireNamespace("mvtnorm", quietly = TRUE)   # for adj = "mvt"
```

`predictmeans()` gives the means of a model term and all their pairwise comparisons.
This vignette shows what to use when the questions are different: comparisons with a
control, trends, tests of several contrasts at once, slopes of a covariate, and other
adjustments for multiple testing. The results match emmeans, pbkrtest and lmerTest
(Kenward–Roger and Satterthwaite) and SAS `LSMEANS`, `SLICE` and `ESTIMATE` statements.

We use the oats split plot again: three varieties on whole plots within six blocks, four
nitrogen levels on subplots.

```{r}
library(predictmeans)
Oats <- as.data.frame(nlme::Oats)
Oats$N <- factor(Oats$nitro)
fm <- lmer(yield ~ N * Variety + (1 | Block/Variety), data = Oats)
```

## Adjusting for multiple comparisons

`adj` sets how the p-values of the pairwise comparisons are adjusted. Besides the
`p.adjust()` methods (`"holm"`, `"BH"`, `"bonferroni"`, ...) and `"tukey"`, there are
`"sidak"`, `"scheffe"` and `"mvt"`. `"mvt"` is the single-step multivariate t
adjustment: it uses the correlations among the comparisons, so it is exact for any
family of contrasts. It is what SAS `ADJUST=SIMULATE` estimates by simulation; here it
is computed by package mvtnorm.

```{r, eval = has_mvt}
p <- sapply(c("none", "tukey", "mvt", "sidak", "scheffe", "holm"), function(a)
  predictmeans(fm, "N", adj = a, plot = FALSE, prtnum = FALSE)$pairs$p.adj)
pm <- predictmeans(fm, "N", plot = FALSE, prtnum = FALSE)
data.frame(pair = paste(pm$pairs$level1, "-", pm$pairs$level2), signif(p, 3))
```

For all pairs of means Tukey and `"mvt"` agree, up to the accuracy of the mvtnorm
computation (about 1e-4, which shows only for very small p-values); `"mvt"` also covers
other families, as below. Scheffé protects every possible contrast and is the most
conservative.

## Families of contrasts

`contrast_family()` builds standard sets of contrasts among the means of a term, with
the same coefficients and names as emmeans: `"pairwise"`, `"revpairwise"`,
`"trt.vs.ctrl"`, `"consec"`, `"poly"`, `"eff"` and `"del.eff"`. The result goes to
`contrastmeans()`.

Each nitrogen level against no nitrogen (Dunnett's comparisons), with the exact Dunnett
adjustment:

```{r}
K <- Kmatrix(fm, "N")
dunnett <- contrast_family(K, "trt.vs.ctrl")
dunnett
```

```{r, eval = has_mvt}
contrastmeans(fm, "N", ctrmatrix = dunnett, adj = "mvt")[[1]]
```

Linear and quadratic trends in nitrogen within each variety (`by`), with integer
orthogonal polynomial coefficients (the nitrogen levels are equally spaced):

```{r}
K2 <- Kmatrix(fm, "N:Variety")
trends <- contrast_family(K2, "poly", by = "Variety", max.degree = 2)
contrastmeans(fm, "N:Variety", ctrmatrix = trends)[[1]]
```

`specify_contrast()` (see the getting-started vignette) writes any other contrast by
the names of the means.

## Joint tests and slices

`pm_joint()` tests several contrasts at once with an F test. With `by`, it compares the
means of the term within each level of the `by` factor, which is SAS
`LSMEANS N*Variety / SLICE=Variety`:

```{r}
pm_joint(fm, "N:Variety", by = "Variety")
pm_joint(fm, "N:Variety", by = "N")
```

The first table asks whether nitrogen matters within each variety, the second whether
the varieties differ at each nitrogen level. With `ctrmatrix`, the rows of any contrast
matrix are tested together, e.g. the departure from a straight line (quadratic and cubic
terms):

```{r}
curv <- contrast_family(K, "poly")[c("quadratic", "cubic"), ]
pm_joint(fm, "N", ctrmatrix = curv)
```

For REML `lmer` fits the test is the Kenward–Roger F test (as `pbkrtest::KRmodcomp()`);
`df_method = "Satterthwaite"` gives lmerTest's test, and `"containment"` the SAS
containment df.

`contrastmeans(..., joint = TRUE)` adds the same joint test to the t tests of the
individual contrasts (and, with a `permlist`, a permutation p-value of the joint F):

```{r}
contrastmeans(fm, "N", ctrmatrix = curv, joint = TRUE)[["Joint F test of the contrasts"]]
```

## Slopes of a covariate

When nitrogen is used as a number, the question is how fast yield rises with it in each
variety. `pm_slopes()` gives the slopes with standard errors, df, confidence limits and
tests, and compares them (as `emmeans::emtrends()`):

```{r}
fm2 <- lmer(yield ~ nitro * Variety + (1 | Block/Variety), data = Oats)
pm_slopes(fm2, "nitro", "Variety", adj = "tukey")
```

The slopes are in yield per unit of nitrogen. With `poly()` or spline terms the slope
changes along the covariate; `at` sets where it is taken (the default is the
covariate's mean).

## Any contrast from `coef()` and `vcov()`

`coef()` and `vcov()` give the means of a `predictmeans()` result and their covariance
matrix (Kenward–Roger adjusted for REML `lmer` fits), named by the levels. Any contrast
can be computed from them:

```{r}
pmv <- predictmeans(fm, "N:Variety", plot = FALSE, prtnum = FALSE)
b <- coef(pmv)
L <- (names(b) == "0.6:Victory") - (names(b) == "0.6:Golden Rain")
c(estimate = sum(L * b), SE = sqrt(drop(L %*% vcov(pmv) %*% L)))
```

They also let other packages test contrasts of the means. marginaleffects needs the
class listed first; `b1`, `b2`, ... are the means in the order of `coef()`:

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("marginaleffects", quietly = TRUE)}
options(marginaleffects_model_classes = "predictmeans")
i <- match(c("0.6:Victory", "0.6:Golden Rain"), names(b))
marginaleffects::hypotheses(pmv, hypothesis = sprintf("b%d - b%d = 0", i[1], i[2]))
```

marginaleffects uses normal-based tests; the standard error is the same as above.

## Equivalence tests

To show that two treatments do not differ by more than a margin that matters in practice,
give the margin with `equivalence` (a number `d` for the region `-d` to `d`, or
`c(lower, upper)`). The `pairs` table then has `p.equiv`, the p-value of two one-sided t
tests (TOST): below `level`, the difference lies within the margin.

```{r}
pe <- predictmeans(fm, "N", equivalence = 15, plot = FALSE, prtnum = FALSE)
pe$pairs[, c("level1", "level2", "estimate", "std.error", "p.equiv")]
```

`contrastmeans(..., equivalence = )` does the same for contrasts.

## Robust and clustered standard errors

When the error variance differs between groups and the model assumes it is constant,
`vcov = "HC3"` (or `"HC0"` to `"HC2"`) gives heteroscedasticity-consistent standard
errors for `lm`, `aov` and `glm` models, and `vcov = ~ Block` cluster-robust ones. They
work in `predictmeans()`, `contrastmeans()`, `pm_slopes()` and `pm_joint()`; the df stay
the model's:

```{r}
fl <- lm(yield ~ Block + N + Variety, data = Oats)
pmh <- predictmeans(fl, "N", vcov = "HC3", plot = FALSE, prtnum = FALSE)
pmh$pairs[, c("level1", "level2", "estimate", "std.error", "p.value")]
pmh$settings$vcov
contrastmeans(fl, "N", ctrmatrix = rbind(c(-1, 1, 0, 0), c(0, -1, 1, 0)), vcov = ~ Block)[[1]]
```

For any model, including mixed models, `vcov` also takes a covariance matrix of the
coefficients or a function that returns one (e.g. from the clubSandwich package).
